name: Tulobuterol
lead: Tulobuterol is a long-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist best known as the active ingredient in a once-daily skin patch (Hokunalin Tape) approved in Japan in 1998 for asthma and COPD.[1] In looksmaxxing and fat-loss circles it is discussed as a patch-form relative of clenbuterol-type beta agonists, which people associate with fat loss and a leaner look.

The patch was the first bronchodilator delivered through the skin. It releases the drug slowly so that the peak blood level coincides with the early-morning dip in lung function while avoiding high peaks that cause systemic side effects.[1] Pharmacokinetic work found a lag of about 4 hours after application and a peak at roughly 9 to 12 hours.[2] A survey of 1,470 patients found 83.2% of transdermal users with asthma reported taking treatment as prescribed, against 52.7% of inhaler users.[3]
Published research is medical: asthma, COPD, cough and perioperative breathing events in children. No published study found here examines tulobuterol for body composition.

chain: Beta agonists are associated with raised metabolic rate and fat mobilisation
angle.text: People discuss tulobuterol as a milder, patch-delivered member of the beta-agonist family used for cutting. Its approved use is bronchodilation; the fat-loss idea is an extrapolation from the drug class.

infobox: Transdermal patch; also oral and aerosol forms

paras: The patch is prescribed in Japan for bronchial asthma and COPD, applied once daily.[1] It has been used for nocturnal and early-morning symptoms, and trials have combined it with the inhaled anticholinergic tiotropium in COPD.[4][5] A bioequivalence study compared the Bretol and Hokunalin 2 mg patches in healthy volunteers.[6]

Other trials include a placebo-controlled study of the patch for respiratory adverse events in 188 children undergoing tonsillectomy, and a study in young children with acute asthma exacerbations.[7][8]

Tulobuterol is a non-catechol beta-2 agonist, so it is not broken down by MAO or COMT; it is conjugated mainly with sulfate in humans.[9] Beta-2 agonists commonly cause tremor and palpitations, which the transdermal design aims to reduce by avoiding peak concentrations.[1][10]
Analytical chemistry papers list tulobuterol among the beta-agonists screened for in urine and meat samples.[11]
Registered studies cover COPD with tiotropium and paediatric tonsillectomy.[12][13] No studies on fat loss or body composition were found.

timeline.event: A clinical review describes tulobuterol in managing obstructive airways disease in adults.[10]
The tulobuterol patch (Hokunalin Tape) is first approved in Japan.[1]
A survey study reports higher adherence with the patch than with inhalers.[3]

card.summary: A once-daily beta-2 agonist skin patch approved in Japan for asthma, discussed in fat-loss circles as a gentler cousin of clenbuterol-type compounds.
card.note: Prescription bronchodilator; beta agonists can cause tremor and palpitations.

quick.overview:
Tulobuterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist delivered through a skin patch, approved in Japan since 1998 for asthma and COPD.

In fat-loss discussions it is mentioned alongside other beta agonists that people associate with a leaner look. Its published research is entirely about breathing conditions.
quick.mechanism: It stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, relaxing airway muscle. The patch releases the drug slowly, peaking around 9 to 12 hours after application, which smooths blood levels.
quick.risks: Typical beta-2 agonist effects include tremor and palpitations. It is a prescription drug where approved and is on lists of beta-agonists screened for in testing programmes.
